parts.name: Queen Amalia's garden
parts.stand: At the main entrance on Amalias Avenue, among the tall palms, facing into the garden.

paras.t: Welcome to the National Garden, right behind the Parliament building. It used to be the Royal Garden. Queen Amalia commissioned it in 1838, and it was finished by 1840. Those palms around the entrance? The entrance was moved here to the 12 palms she planted, in her honor.
If the city is hot today, you've come to the right place. One travel guide calls this easily the coolest place to hide from the summer sun.

It was laid out by a German agronomist, Friedrich Schmidt. He brought in over 500 kinds of plants, and peacocks, ducks and turtles too. Sadly a lot of the plants couldn't take the dry Mediterranean climate and died. For a long time part of it was the private refuge of the King and Queen. People could already visit in the afternoons; in the 1920s it was opened to the public as a park, and in time it took the name National Garden.

parts.name: Inside the garden
parts.stand: Follow the paths into the garden, and stop wherever you find shade.

paras.t: Keep your eyes open as you wander. There are ancient ruins tucked in among the trees, mostly Roman: columns, and even a Roman villa with a mosaic. There's a duck pond, and look out for the turtles and the tortoises that live here.
Look out, too, for the busts. One is of Ioannis Kapodistrias, the first governor of Greece. Another is the poet Dionysios Solomos, who wrote the words of the Greek national anthem.

Now a very strange story. In 1920, King Alexander was bitten by a pet monkey, and about three weeks later he died of the infection. One account says it happened here in the garden; we're not sure of that.

His death brought back his deposed father, King Constantine. Historians have argued that the political change that followed helped lead to Greece's defeat in Asia Minor, the disaster Greeks call the Catastrophe. Winston Churchill wrote that perhaps a quarter of a million people died of this monkey's bite.

parts.name: The Zappeion
parts.stand: Take the gate that leads from the garden into the Zappeion park, and face the large building.

paras.t: This grand building is the Zappeion. It was the first building ever put up specifically for the revival of the Olympic Games. It was designed by Theophil Hansen and opened on October 20, 1888.

It's named for Evangelis Zappas, who had started his own Zappian Olympic Games, a forerunner of the modern Olympics. He paid for this, but didn't live to see it built. And here's an odd detail: his head is said to be buried inside one of the building's walls.

At the 1896 Olympics this was the main fencing hall, and in 1906 it housed the athletes. In 1938 Greece's first national radio station started broadcasting from here. And in May 1979, in its marble atrium, Greece signed the papers to join the European Community.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: Find a bench in the shade before you leave.

paras.t: The writer Henry Miller, writing in 1939, said this garden stayed in his memory like no other park he had known. He called it the quintessence of a park. Sit a minute before you go back into the traffic. That's what this garden has been for, ever since the gates opened to everyone.
